With 815 horsepower from its supercharged Predator 5.2-liter V-8 engine, the roadgoing car has far more power than the Mustang GT3 race car it shares styling with. That track-only model instead uses a 5.4-liter V-8 with around 550 horsepower. Cog swaps for the GTD come courtesy of a rear-mounted eight-speed dual-clutch automated transaxle, similar to the type of gearbox used in the race car.

A Mustang GTD we tested blew us away with its performance. Its shockingly civilized on-road ride quality surprised us as well. We would welcome more steering feedback, but the supremely balanced handling and staggering levels of grip make for a world-class driving experience.

In Comparison: The Mustang GTD is quick, but two other rear-drive rockets, the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 and Porsche 911 GT3 RS, outran it to 60 mph in our testing, completing that task in 2.2 and 2.7 seconds, respectively.

The Ford Mustang GTD prioritizes lap times over fuel economy, as the roar from its mighty supercharged V-8 quickly reveals. As a result, the GTD only manages a pitiful 10 mpg in the city, 17 mpg on the highway, and 12 mpg combined, according to the EPA. For more information about the Mustang GTD's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

First Row: Though it looks every bit like the Mustang GT3 purpose-built race car on the outside, the GTD's cabin looks a lot like any ol' Mustang's. Suede, leather, and carbon fiber are the main ingredients of the GTD's interior that upgrade it from its lesser kin—though not by much. Recaro bucket seats hug both driver and front passenger, but the GTD jettisons the rear seats of other Mustang models. The paddle shifters are 3D-printed from titanium, same for the rotary dial gear selector and serial placard. Ford claims it sourced the material for these components from retired Lockheed Martin F-22 fighter jets.

Cargo Capacity: The trunk is a treasure box of suspension and cooling components, but there is room for some small pieces of soft luggage where the rear seat used to be.

The Mustang GTD packs a 12.4-inch digital gauge cluster and a 13.2-inch touchscreen infotainment display. Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are standard equipment. Though the system is largely the same as that of other Mustangs, it does include additional GTD-exclusive performance menus.

As you'd expect of a car like this, the GTD doesn't have many driver-assistance features, but it does have a lane-keep assist system and automatic emergency braking.

For information about the GTD's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

The Mustang GTD has a solid but average warranty. However, unlike rival Chevy, Ford doesn't provide a complimentary scheduled maintenance visit.

#4267. Study of 750,000 pregnancies reveals a surprising twist about Ozempic and Wegovy

A major study involving more than 750,000 pregnancies has uncovered an important difference in the potential pregnancy risks of popular weight loss medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. Women who unintentionally used these drugs shortly before or during early pregnancy were more likely to give birth prematurely, but only when the medications had been prescribed to treat existing diabetes.

Among women taking the same medications for weight management, researchers found no significant association with premature birth or other pregnancy complications examined in the study.

The findings suggest that diabetes itself, rather than the medications, may be responsible for the increased risk of early delivery. The research was published in Human Reproduction Open, a leading journal in reproductive medicine.

The medications examined included semaglutide (brand names: Ozempic, Wegovy) and liraglutide (Saxenda). Both belong to a widely used group of drugs known as GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs). Originally developed to manage type 2 diabetes, these medications also suppress appetite, making them effective treatments for weight loss. However, their safety during pregnancy has not been established.

Why Ozempic and Similar Drugs Raise Pregnancy Concerns

Professor Henriette Svarre Nielsen, who led the research at the Department of Gynecology and Obstetrics at Copenhagen University Hospital Hvidovre in Hvidovre, Denmark, explained that the rapid rise in GLP-1 prescriptions has created an urgent need for better information about pregnancy exposure.

"GLP-1 RA treatment has, within the last few years, become the medication with the sharpest increase in prescriptions worldwide. Current guidance suggests the treatment should be stopped eight weeks prior to planning a pregnancy. However, this is based on early-phase model organism studies, and not real-world evidence. Nonetheless, because of its widespread adoption, inadvertent exposure in early pregnancy is inevitable, and there is hardly any evidence to guide clinical counseling when it happens."

To investigate these concerns, researchers examined whether accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications around conception was associated with complications during pregnancy. They focused on preterm birth (birth before 37 weeks), pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes, delivering a baby that was unusually large for its gestational age, stillbirth, and placental problems.

Study Examines More Than 750,000 Pregnancies

The research team used Denmark's nationwide health registries to examine 756,636 pregnancies involving a single baby among 480,231 women. All pregnancies resulted in deliveries between October 1, 2009, and December 31, 2023.

The researchers classified a pregnancy as having possible accidental exposure to GLP-1 medications if the woman filled a prescription for semaglutide or liraglutide during the eight weeks before or after the first day of her last menstrual period.

This 16-week period included the time when a woman might not yet realize she was pregnant, as well as the early stages of fetal development when major organs begin to form.

Of the pregnancies included in the study, 529 involved prescription records indicating exposure to GLP-1 medications during this period.

To make the comparisons more reliable, the researchers accounted for several characteristics that could influence pregnancy outcomes. These included maternal age, body mass index (BMI), smoking habits, location, education, and whether the woman already had diabetes. They also considered the month and year of pregnancy to account for possible seasonal patterns and changes over time.

Diabetes May Be the Key to Premature Birth Risk

The results revealed a striking distinction between women prescribed GLP-1 drugs for diabetes and those using them for weight loss.

Dr. Kathrine Hviid, the study's first author and a PhD student in the same department, said the findings could help shape future research and improve medical guidance for women who unknowingly use these drugs during early pregnancy.

"We made some extremely important findings that have implications for future studies, such as randomized controlled trials of GLP-1 RA usage in pregnancy, and for clinical counseling.

"We found that these medications were associated with an increased risk of preterm birth, but the risk was only present when the medication was used for diabetes treatment, and not for weight management. This suggests that the underlying condition of diabetes, rather than the medication, may be driving this association."

At first, women with GLP-1 prescriptions appeared to experience several pregnancy complications more frequently than those without exposure. However, most of these associations were no longer statistically significant once the researchers accounted for other factors that could affect pregnancy outcomes.

The remaining significant association involved premature birth among women who had been prescribed liraglutide or semaglutide to manage diabetes.

Compared with women who had not been exposed to these medications, the adjusted odds of premature delivery were 70% higher among women taking liraglutide for diabetes and 84% higher among those taking semaglutide for diabetes.

The researchers' accompanying announcement also reported estimated increases of approximately 11% for semaglutide and 9% for liraglutide among women with pre-existing diabetes.

Crucially, the same elevated risk of premature birth was not observed when the medications were prescribed specifically for weight management.

This difference suggests that the underlying medical condition may play a larger role in pregnancy outcomes than exposure to the medications themselves.

What the Findings Mean for Women Taking GLP-1 Drugs

According to Professor Nielsen, future investigations must distinguish between women taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes and those using them for weight control. Combining these groups could obscure important differences in their underlying health and pregnancy risks.

"Future studies must take account of the reason a woman has been prescribed these medications, as the risks differ between women using GLP-1 RAs for diabetes versus weight management. This is one of the first studies to examine GLP-1 RA exposure in early pregnancy according to the reason for prescription. As more evidence accumulates, these findings will guide clinical counseling for women inadvertently exposed to GLP-1 RAs in early pregnancy. In Denmark, about 70% of people who use weight loss medications are women and so it is inevitable that some may take it without realizing they are pregnant."

Although the results provide useful new information, Nielsen emphasized that additional research is necessary before changing existing medical recommendations.

In particular, the findings do not justify abandoning current guidance to discontinue GLP-1 medications before a planned pregnancy. They also do not provide enough evidence to establish new clinical counseling recommendations based on why the drugs were prescribed.

Important Limitations of the Pregnancy Study

One of the investigation's greatest strengths was its size, with health records covering more than three-quarters of a million pregnancies.

However, the study was observational, meaning it could identify associations but could not determine whether GLP-1 medications directly caused premature births. Other factors, including the effects of diabetes itself, may help explain the results.

Another limitation was that the researchers relied on prescription records. Although they could determine whether a woman had filled a prescription, they could not confirm whether she had actually taken the medication.

The researchers nevertheless believe that most women who purchased the drugs were likely to have used them because of their substantial cost.

In Denmark, patients generally contribute toward the cost of GLP-1 injections, although government subsidies are available for diabetes treatment. For example, a 1mg injection of Wegovy or Ozempic (semaglutide) costs approximately €180 and €114, respectively, with the diabetes subsidy reflected in the lower price.

Dr. Hviid said: "Because of the high cost, we assume that compliance is very high among the women prescribed GLP-1 RAs."

Experts Call for More Individualized Pregnancy Guidance

The findings also attracted attention from researchers outside Denmark.

In an invited commentary published alongside the study, Drs. Yeyi Zhu and Monique Hedderson of Kaiser Permanente Northern California and the Center for Upstream Prevention of Adiposity and Diabetes Mellitus in Pleasanton, California, described the results as important additions to the growing research on GLP-1 medications and reproductive health.

They wrote that the findings "complement and extend an emerging evidence base on the reproductive safety of GLP-1 RAs."

The researchers also emphasized that the distinction between diabetes treatment and weight management could help doctors provide more personalized advice to women who accidentally used these medications around conception.

"For clinicians, the study by Hviid et al. (2026) may inform preconception and early pregnancy counseling. The observation that elevated preterm birth risk was confined to women treated for diabetes, and not to those using GLP-1 receptor agonists for weight management, supports more balanced, individualized discussions with patients who may have experienced inadvertent periconceptional exposure. For patients with diabetes, the study reinforces the importance of recognizing diabetes as an important risk factor for obstetric complications and prioritizing metabolic health and glycemic management before and during pregnancy."

Ultimately, the study highlights why a woman's underlying health conditions matter when evaluating the potential pregnancy risks of GLP-1 medications. While the findings offer some reassurance regarding accidental exposure among women using these drugs for weight loss, they do not establish that the medications are safe during pregnancy.

Further research will be needed to clarify the risks and determine how best to counsel women who become pregnant while using these increasingly popular treatments.

Materials provided by European Society of Human Reproduction and Embryology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4266. 10 Games That Have Creative Punishments for Cheating

Shane is a Contributor for DualShockers writing guides and other materials. He has a degree in Game Design and Criticism.

It’ll come as no surprise to any gamer that pretty much every game has a way to cheat, whether it's approved by the developers or otherwise. Over the years there have been some pretty creative and hilarious ways that developers have dealt with cheaters in all kinds of games from FPS games to the cozy ones.

While a lot of the punishments for cheating in more recent years are typical things like warnings or outright bans, there are some that take a more creative approach. Whether it’s a fun way to kill the player or an incredibly punishing turn of events for dark deeds, it’s always funny to see that happen.

This list consists of many games from all sorts of genres and ages, but they all have some interesting and hilarious punishments for what they perceive as cheating. It may not always be altering game files and could just be something players are able to abuse in game.

Way back in 1996 Crusader: No Regret came out following in the footsteps of its predecessor Crusader: No Remorse. The isometric gameplay combined with some great weapons and destructive environments made a very engaging combination.

The only problem was if you played the previous game and attempted to use any cheats from the last game Crusader: No Regret would have something to say about it. Players would be greeted with a message and teleported into a room with eight copies of the final boss.

Heretic was created using the DOOM engine, but things were a bit mixed up and instead of the traditional DOOM world this one was steeped in fantasy elements. Everything revolved around the fantasy element as players could use magical weapons like the Elven Wand, and Phoenix Rod.

Unfortunately for players who were well educated in the ways of DOOM, the developers had a surprise for anyone hoping to use DOOM cheats. Inserting the cheat for God Mode would instantly kill players, and the all weapons cheat would instead reduce you to using just a wooden staff.

With the recent remaster of Ocarina of Time there’s a lot of great details in the Legend of Zelda series coming to light. Some are just fun little tidbits or small things, but in Link’s Awakening the dev team decided to make things a little harder for anyone doing nefarious things with Link.

Link can steal some items from a shopkeeper by distracting him and then grabbing the items to take outside. Not only does doing this ruin Link’s reputation earning him the mark of thief by any other NPCs, that shopkeeper will also kill Link to settle the debt.

Activision is drawing a line in the sand against third party lobby shopping apps, threatening bans outright.

Traditional MMOs typically don’t play too well with cheaters, resulting in all kinds of punishments, but one MMO really stands out, EVE Online. This old school MMORPG is all about space battles and exploration in its entirely player driven world.

During a GM Week event there were public executions of cheaters who had been caught and the team opened up the destruction of these ships to any players who wanted to join. This turned it into an incredible spectacle that many will not soon forget.

The Sims series is probably one of the most prolific gaming franchises on the planet, being enjoyed by a huge demographic of people. Even in these cute games people try to cheat and The Sims devs were not going to let that slide even on the DS.

If you attempted to use the internal system clock to skip time forward the game would notice and spawn an alien invasion that would cause a lot of problems. They become a persistent problem in the game and could require players to restart the game.

To combat rampant cheating, BULKHEAD implements ping locks to keep certain regions out of main servers.

CD Projekt Red are known for their storytelling and incredible game design, but they don’t just stop being amazing there. While the devs respect when players are able to find something they hadn’t accounted for they didn’t stop them from doing it, they just got a bit creative.

When The Witcher 3 originally came out there was an exploit that would let you kill cows in the starter area indefinitely giving you crazy amounts of money. To fix that they simply spawned a giant late game monster, a Chort, that would likely kill players as a punishment.

There’s nothing quite like finding out a classic game has punishments for attempted cheating, and Pokemon Ruby and Sapphire is no exception. Despite being a game for mostly young people they weren’t going to stand by and let someone cheat in their game.

Pokemon, of course, has a way to mess with players who were able to manipulate game code although it's a bit different from others on the list. Instead of anything dangerous the game would spawn a Bad Egg in a box that cannot be moved creating an issue with inventory for the rest of the game.

Cheat codes in games have been around for longer than most gamers, so a lot of early games allowed players to put them in. Now just like some other games, they want to encourage you to still play the regular way and have to get a bit more creative about punishments.

Banjo-Kazooie took this to an extreme and offered players the ability to put in forbidden codes doing all kinds of silly things. If you put in too many Gruntilda will threaten to erase your save file, making this a very dangerous gamble if you aren’t careful.

A config exploit is helping losers disconnect from Marvel Rivals matches without penalties.

Edmund can’t ever do something in half measures and Mewgenics is more than proof of that in almost every aspect. The game took a lot of things to extremes and dealing with cheaters is no exception.

If you tried to save-scum, quitting out of something quickly to reload a previous save, the game would know and you’d meet Steven. The first time you do this in a run he gives you a warning, but if you continue to do it you’ll no longer have control of the game and Steven will make all the choices.

Not many games have the sense of humor that The Stanley Parable has and this, of course, has to extend beyond the metaness of the game. This hilarious narrative game wants you to focus on the order of events and not have you screw that all up.

If a player attempts to use console cheats the game takes notice and sends them to the Serious Room where the narrator has some choice words for them. Continuing to do it only makes the punishment longer and more ridiculous, much like everything in the game.

From giant heads to low gravity, these are the PS2 Games That Had the Most Ridiculous Cheat Codes — and Why Players Still Miss Them.

#4264. AI supercharges laser physics with a stunning 250x speed boost

Simulating the complex behavior of light inside powerful laser systems requires enormous computing resources, making it difficult for researchers to predict and adjust laser performance quickly. Now, scientists at Stanford University, the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), and SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory have developed an artificial intelligence model that dramatically accelerates these calculations. Using deep learning, the new approach reproduces the results of conventional simulations in a fraction of the time while maintaining high accuracy across a wide variety of laser pulse shapes.

The advance focuses on a branch of physics called second-order nonlinear optics, also known as χ2 processes. These interactions occur when light waves exchange energy while traveling through specially designed crystals, allowing scientists to change the frequency of light and precisely control the shape of laser pulses. Such capabilities are particularly important at large scientific facilities that use lasers to generate intense X-rays.

How Laser Light Helps Generate Powerful X-Rays

At SLAC's upgraded Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS-II), laser pulses undergo a series of transformations before they can help produce X-rays. Infrared light is first converted into green light and then into ultraviolet (UV) light. The resulting UV pulse strikes a cathode, releasing a cluster of electrons that is accelerated and manipulated to generate powerful X-ray pulses.

The precise timing and shape of the UV pulse help determine the characteristics of the electron bunch. Those characteristics, in turn, influence the quality of the X-rays that researchers use in scientific experiments. Accurately predicting the conversion of light between different frequencies is therefore an important part of optimizing the system.

The new AI approach, described in the journal Advanced Photonics, was developed specifically to model the nonlinear χ2 interactions involved in this frequency conversion process.

AI Replaces Time-Consuming Laser Calculations

Traditionally, scientists simulate these interactions by solving a complex mathematical equation known as the nonlinear Schrödinger equation. A widely used technique called the split-step Fourier method (SSFM) calculates how light changes as it travels through a material, repeatedly switching between representations of the pulse in time and frequency.

Although the method produces accurate results, it demands substantial computing power. In the complete laser simulation examined by the researchers, this calculation alone accounts for approximately 95 percent of the total processing time.

To overcome that bottleneck, the team developed an AI model based on a type of recurrent neural network called LSTM (long short-term memory). Building on earlier research that used similar networks to predict how laser pulses travel through optical fibers, the scientists adapted the approach to handle more complicated interactions involving multiple light waves.

They tested the model using a process called noncollinear sum frequency generation, or SFG, in which three interconnected light fields evolve together inside a crystal. The simulations covered a wide variety of laser pulse shapes, providing a demanding test of the model's ability to reproduce complex optical behavior.

One important innovation was the way the AI handles information. Rather than repeatedly converting calculations between time and frequency, as conventional simulations do, the neural network works entirely with a compressed representation of the light's frequency characteristics. This eliminates much of the repetitive computation that makes traditional methods slow.

Complex Laser Simulations in Just Milliseconds

The results showed that the AI model could accurately recreate how laser pulses change over time and across different frequencies, even under particularly challenging conditions. These included pulses with pronounced gaps in their frequency spectra and strong variations in optical phase.

When the researchers processed multiple simulations together using graphics processing units, the average calculation time for each simulation dropped to just a few milliseconds. That represents an improvement of orders of magnitude over conventional methods, making it possible to obtain predictions far more quickly without substantially compromising accuracy.

The system also demonstrated an important ability to capture the interconnected behavior of the light waves. When the AI accurately predicted the main output of the SFG process, its predictions for the other interacting fields were generally accurate as well. This suggests that the network learned important features of the overall interaction rather than simply reproducing one output.

Toward Smarter Lasers and Real-Time Control

Beyond faster simulations, the researchers envision connecting AI models directly to operating laser systems. Their approach uses a modular design in which individual physical processes can be represented by separate trained neural networks. Combining these models could make it possible to predict the behavior of an entire experimental system while it is running.

One potential application is the creation of digital twins, detailed virtual models that mirror the behavior of real laser equipment. With sufficiently fast and accurate predictions, these systems could help researchers monitor experiments, anticipate changes, and adjust laser settings in response to changing conditions.

The technology could also support adaptive laser control and closer integration with diagnostic instruments that measure the results of experiments. By removing a major computational obstacle, the research brings the possibility of more responsive, precisely controlled laser systems closer to reality, with potential benefits for a wide range of scientific facilities that rely on powerful lasers.

Materials provided by SPIE--International Society for Optics and Photonics. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4262. Diablo 4's long-awaited Tower and its Leaderboards enter beta today, and there's no PTR funny business this time

Diablo 4's first big moment of 2026 is nearly upon us, and it's one feature many have been looking forward to for actual years.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside update 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

The beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

The Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

#4260. 10 Great Games That Defined The Xbox 360

Eric Warner is a Journalist and Multimedia Producer based in New England with over 7 years of experience producing stories for multiple publications

November 2026 will see the original Xbox consoles and the overall Xbox brand celebrate its 25th anniversary. and while many gamers will surely be reminiscing their time playing on the sixth gen console, this month should also be a time to celebrate Xbox’s other eras.

Without a doubt, the most prosperous era of the Xbox brand was that of the Xbox 360, as it was not only the go-to home console for hardcore gamers of the time but the 360 was also home to numerous innovative exclusive titles, software, and hardware.

In celebration of the Xbox’s brand’s 25th anniversary, here’s a look back at 10 exclusive Xbox 360 games that defined the console and Microsoft’s brief time at the top of the gaming market.

As mentioned before, the 360 era was a very experimental era for Xbox hardware and this was best represented by the innovative hands-free motion capture camera sensor, the Kinect, with arguably its most famous game being Kinect Star Wars.

In many ways, the Kinect was Microsoft’s answer to the Nintendo Wii and to help compete against the Wii, Microsoft published several promising motion titles such as Kinect Star Wars, allowing people to play a Jedi, Podrace, and wreak chaos as a Rancor all with just their hand and body movements.

Sure, Kinect Star Wars has become sort of a joke over the years, thanks in large part to its Just Dance-like Galactic Dance Off, but it’s still arguably the best game on the 360 to showcase the potential and capabilities of the Kinect.

Project Gotham Racing and Forza Motorsport were the go-to exclusive racing games for Xbox players for several years. While they were fun, neither series allowed players to freely drive in an open-world, an issue Microsoft chose to rectify in the Forza spinoff game Forza Horizon.

Set in Colorado during the Horizon Festival street racing event, Forza Horizon had players take part in the Festival’s formal street races using over 200 cars, as well as challenge other players and even planes and helicopters to informal races throughout the state.

This free style racing design and its vast array of customization options made Forza Horizon an instant hit, leading developer Playground Games to create multiple Horizon sequels and even eclipse Motorsport to become Xbox’s definitive exclusive racing franchise.

In 2002, Microsoft acquired the beloved British game developer Rare for $375 million, and while they would only release two games for the original Xbox, they would develop several titles exclusively for the Xbox 360. Arguably the best was Viva Piñata.

A first-person life simulation game, Viva Piñata was one of the most unique titles offered exclusively on the 360, as it centered around players restoring a garden on Piñata Island to attract adorable local piñata-themed animals to farm, breed, and defend before ultimately sending them to parties.

Viva Piñata is still to this very day widely considered to be the best new IP Rare created under Microsoft, and while the series has laid dormant for years following the release of a sequel and two spinoffs, it's still fondly remembered by many for its creative designs, comedy, and unique gameplay routine.

From Project Gotham Racing to Halo: Combat Evolved, these 10 great games defined the original Xbox and set the groundwork for Xbox's future.

One of the best exclusive original Xbox RPGs was Lionhead Studios’ Fable. Sadly, it didn’t completely live up to series creator Peter Molyneux’s claims and hype, though the series would slowly start to achieve all of Molyneux’s promises in the sequel, Fable II.

Set roughly 500 years after the first game in a newly industrial iteration of Albion, Fable II has players embody an orphan known as Sparrow as they grow to become a new hero, destined to save Albion from the ruthless Lord Lucien.

As of this writing, Fable II is Fable at its best, as not only does it feature an intriguing fantasy, industrial world but it features several new and immersive mechanics such as a permanent dog companion, flintlock style firearms, local and online two-player co-op, and allowing players to have children.

The Xbox 360 wasn’t as powerful as the PlayStation 3 on paper, but the Microsoft console was far easier to develop games for than the Sony platform, leading many companies to develop their titles exclusively for the 360. One such game was Capcom’s Dead Rising.

Zombie games had been common for a while by the time of Dead Rising’s 2006 launch, but DR was the first zombie game to properly depict massive zombie hordes that had only appeared in books and films beforehand, with literally thousands of zombies filling the Willamette Mall.

On top of these huge herds of the undead, Dead Rising further showcased the power of the 360 by allowing the game’s protagonist, Frank West, to slay zombies with practically every object found in the mall, such as jugs of orange juice, CDs, katanas, shopping carts, lawnmowers, and more.

BioWare and Microsoft formed a strong relationship during the original Xbox era by releasing Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic and Jade Empire exclusively for the sixth gen console. This relationship continued briefly into the 360 era, with the launch of Mass Effect.

Inspired by Star Wars, Mass Effect was BioWare’s most ambitious project, as it introduced several new mechanics that have since become mainstays in RPGs, such as real-time, third-person, cover-focused combat, conversational Dialogue Wheel choices, and NPC relationships that would continue into future sequels.

With its expansive sci-fi universe, memorable characters, and easy to understand gameplay, Mass Effect continued to show that both BioWare and Xbox were the undisputed masters of western RPGs, as the innovations made in ME can still be felt in several RPGs today.

The Xbox 360 was a great console, but nostalgia might be blinding us into thinking it was all hits and never misses like these.

2007 is well known to be one of the best years in gaming history, especially for those who owned an Xbox 360, as that year not only saw the launch of Mass Effect, Crackdown, and Lost Odyssey, but also the debut of a true work of gaming art in the form of BioShock.

Released as a timed 360 exclusive, BioShock was a spiritual successor to the FPS System Shock series. Instead of traveling to a space station, BioShock had players journey to a mysterious lighthouse deep below the sea to a hidden mid-20th century underwater city called Rapture full of ruination.

BioShock’s gameplay was fantastic, but what made it really stand out from other games of its era was its environmental design inspired by gothic and art deco concepts and its haunting narrative full of horrors, despair, and twists around every corner.

While the Xbox Live Arcade digital storefront didn’t debut on the 360, Arcade was at its most popular during the 360 era, launching several hit exclusive titles such as Braid, 'Splosion Man, Shadow Complex, and the storefront’s absolute best-seller, Minecraft.

Long before Microsoft acquired Mojang but shortly after Minecraft first debuted on PCs, the hit cubic sandbox game would make its way to consoles for the first time via Xbox Live Arcade in 2012, in the form of Minecraft: Xbox 360 Edition based on Java Edition Beta 1.6.6.

Since then, Minecraft: Xbox 360 Edition paved the way for millions of console players to easily experience Minecraft for the first time, becoming the source of countless memories of friends exploring an infinite number of worlds, testing out new features in every update, and messing around with Mash-Up packs.

These Xbox 360 games featured fantastic co-op gameplay that rewarded those who explored every inch of their levels and world.

The original Xbox’s defining breakout exclusive title was Halo: Combat Evolved and, in 2006, the 360 would receive its own breakout exclusive game in the form of the third-person cover shooter, Gears of War.

With its innovative third-person gameplay, monstrous Locust enemy designs, and iconic chainsaw bayoneted Lancer assault rifle, Gears of War took the gaming world by storm though everything that made the game great would be significantly improved upon in its sequel, Gears of War 2.

To this day, Gears of War 2 is still considered to feature the best Gears campaign in the series but what it truly revolutionary for gaming overall was the introduction of the PvE Horde Mode pitting players against increasingly deadlier waves of enemies, a mode that many other games would go on to improve upon.

As mentioned before, 2007 was an amazing year for the Xbox 360 but the best exclusive game to debut that year and the one title that undoubtedly best defined the 360 console overall was Bungie’s masterpiece, Halo 3.

The epic conclusion to the original Halo trilogy, Halo 3 saw Master Chief and the Arbiter return to Earth and eventually the Forerunner installation known as the Ark as they and joint UNSC and Elite forces set out to wipe out the Covenant and the Flood once and for all.

Halo 3’s campaign was a perfect finale for the Halo series but Bungie introduced so many new features in the game that have made it stand as one of the best FPS titles of all time such as the map editor Forge, Theater Mode, File Share, Grifball, four-player campaign co-op, deployable equipment, and so much more.

These Xbox 360 games are fun from the start to finish and remain that way upon repeat single-player or multiplayer playthroughs.

#4258. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4257. Scientists discover a common sugar may help cancer cells break free and spread

A common sugar found in many foods and sweetened drinks may play an unexpected role in helping aggressive ovarian cancer spread. Researchers at The Wistar Institute have discovered that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy can release fructose, which acts as a signal that encourages nearby tumor cells to break free and spread.

The findings, published in Nature Aging, reveal a previously unknown way that cancer cells can continue influencing a tumor even after treatment has stopped them from multiplying. The discovery also raises important questions about whether dietary sugar and commonly prescribed cholesterol medications could affect how cancer progresses.

"Some cancer cells that survive chemotherapy aren't dividing anymore, but they're still biologically active," said Aidan Cole, Ph.D., a postdoctoral fellow in the lab of Katherine Aird, Ph.D., at The Wistar Institute and first author on the study. "Instead, they continue to release molecules that send signals to nearby cells. Our study is among the first to show that a nutrient -- in this case, fructose -- can act as one of those signals."

Why Ovarian Cancer Often Returns After Chemotherapy

Most patients with ovarian cancer receive platinum-based chemotherapy, a treatment that uses drugs containing platinum to damage the DNA of cancer cells and prevent them from reproducing. Although many patients initially respond well, the cancer eventually returns in most cases. It also frequently spreads throughout the abdominal cavity, the space inside the abdomen that contains organs such as the stomach, intestines, and liver.

This spread, known as metastasis, is responsible for approximately 90% of ovarian cancer deaths. Understanding what allows cancer cells to escape from their original location and establish new tumors is therefore a major priority for researchers.

Previous studies have suggested that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy may contribute to recurrence even when they are no longer actively dividing. These surviving cells can continue producing and releasing a mixture of substances that influence the behavior of surrounding cells.

To investigate this process, Cole and his colleagues developed an experiment that separated the surviving cancer cells from the molecules they released. They discovered that these released substances, even without the surviving cells themselves, were enough to significantly increase cancer spread in a preclinical model.

"As far as we know, this is the first time anyone has shown, in a preclinical model rather than just a dish, that it's the molecules these cells release -- not the cells themselves -- that drive the cancer's spread," said Cole.

A Common Sugar Emerges as a Surprising Cancer Signal

The next challenge was identifying which substances were responsible for encouraging cancer cells to spread. The researchers discovered an unexpected culprit: fructose.

Fructose is a naturally occurring sugar found in fruit, honey, and other foods. It is also a component of table sugar and high fructose corn syrup, a sweetener frequently used in soft drinks and processed foods.

The study revealed that cancer cells surviving chemotherapy could produce fructose and release it into their surroundings. Rather than simply serving as an energy source, the sugar acted as a chemical messenger that encouraged neighboring cancer cells to become more capable of spreading.

The researchers also uncovered another concerning possibility. In their preclinical experiments, consuming high amounts of fructose comparable to those found in sugary drinks could promote signals associated with cancer spread even without chemotherapy treatment.

This observation suggests that diet might influence cancer progression through a mechanism scientists had not previously recognized. Fructose consumption is particularly relevant in the United States, where high fructose corn syrup can account for approximately 8% to 20% of daily calorie intake in some individuals.

Unlike many factors that influence cancer risk and progression, dietary fructose intake can be changed. That raises the possibility that nutritional strategies might eventually become part of efforts to limit cancer spread.

However, researchers have not yet tested whether reducing fructose consumption improves outcomes in patients with ovarian cancer. The findings do not establish that eating sugar causes cancer to spread in humans, and additional research is needed before specific dietary recommendations can be made based on this mechanism.

How Fructose Helps Cancer Cells Break Free

To understand how fructose encourages cancer spread, the researchers examined what happens inside cancer cells exposed to the sugar.

They used several advanced methods to investigate the biological changes involved, including a CRISPR screen. This technique allows scientists to systematically examine genes and identify which ones influence a particular cellular process.

The experiments revealed that fructose suppresses cholesterol production in neighboring cancer cells.

Although cholesterol is often discussed in connection with heart disease, it also serves essential functions throughout the body. It is an important component of cell membranes, the thin outer layers that surround cells and help regulate how they interact with their environment.

In this case, cholesterol helps maintain the connections that hold neighboring cells together. These connections act somewhat like biological glue, making it harder for cancer cells to separate from one another.

When fructose reduces cholesterol production, those connections weaken. As a result, cancer cells can detach more easily, potentially allowing them to escape and spread to other locations.

This discovery provides a possible explanation for how a common nutrient can influence one of the most dangerous aspects of cancer.

A Surprising Connection Between Statins and Cancer Spread

The cholesterol finding also led researchers to investigate an unexpected question involving statins, medications widely prescribed to lower cholesterol.

Approximately 39 million people in the United States take statins. These drugs work by reducing the body's production of cholesterol and are commonly used to lower the risk of heart attacks and strokes.

Because fructose appeared to promote cancer spread by suppressing cholesterol production, the research team wanted to know whether statins might produce similar effects.

Their experiments showed that statins alone could weaken the connections between cancer cells, making it easier for them to separate and escape.

The finding raises questions about whether cholesterol-lowering medications could influence the effectiveness of chemotherapy in certain situations. Researchers are now investigating that possibility, but they emphasize that the results have not been demonstrated in patients and are not a reason for anyone to discontinue prescribed statins.

"We haven't tested this effect in patients yet, but it raises questions about combining cholesterol-lowering drugs with chemotherapy, especially since ovarian cancer is most common in postmenopausal women who are often already on statins," said Katherine Aird, Ph.D., professor and co-leader of the Molecular and Cellular Oncogenesis Program in the Ellen and Ronald Caplan Cancer Center at The Wistar Institute, and senior author of the study.

Could Fructose Also Help Other Cancers Spread?

Although the research focused on ovarian cancer, the scientists suspect that the same biological process could occur in other forms of the disease.

Cancers affecting organs within the abdomen and torso can also spread to nearby tissues and organs. If fructose influences the connections between cancer cells in a similar way, the discovery could have implications beyond ovarian cancer.

"We think other cancers that spread within the torso -- pancreatic, colon, liver -- could behave similarly. We can't call it universal yet, but we think the effects are not just limited to ovarian cancer," said Aird.

Aird and Cole have already begun designing additional experiments to determine whether their findings can be reproduced in pancreatic, colon, liver, and other cancers.

The research opens a new avenue for understanding how cancer spreads, particularly after chemotherapy. It also suggests that the relationship between nutrients, cholesterol production, and cancer cell behavior may be more complicated than previously understood.

While the potential implications for diet and medication remain uncertain, identifying fructose as a signal that helps cancer cells break free could eventually point researchers toward new strategies for preventing metastasis and improving cancer treatment.

#4255. 2027 Scion Kei-01 First Drive: Mite Makes Right

We spent a little bit of time driving a short distance in a tiny pickup that’ll be sold in small numbers.

We haven’t timed one, but eyeballing it, the Scion Kei-01 should reach its top speed before the 1250-hp Chevy Corvette ZR1X reaches 100 mph. (You’re welcome, Toyota marketing team.) Of course, that’s because America’s newest and cutest truck is limited to just 25 mph, per the feds’ FMVSS No. 500 regulation that allows the Kei-01 to be sold here. Toyota is assembling and selling these rebadged Daihatsu Hijets in the United States starting next year, and we got to take one for a short drive—which will be most drives in a pickup this small—to see whether it lives up to the hype.

First, we had to fight our instinct to get into the driver’s seat from the left side. The Kei-01 is right-hand drive, like the Hijet sold in Japan, because Toyota wanted to bring it to the United States as quickly and inexpensively as possible. Production models will get a different backup camera to meet federal requirements, but beyond that, the U.S. version is largely unchanged from the Daihatsu sold in Japan.

See all results for used cars for sale near 19106

Every Kei-01 sold here, mainly to fleets, will have an extended cab, which affords extra cargo space for a shotgun or your largest bushel of chewing tobacco. Or both. The fixed steering column doesn’t tilt or telescope, but stovepipe-hat enthusiasts—and it’s been a while since they’ve heard this—have reason to celebrate, as the one thing this truck does big is headroom.

The Kei-01’s “jumbo” cab is why it stands just 2.9 inches lower in height than an F-150, but it’s a lot easier to get into. You barely have to lift a foot to climb in. A portion of the footwell is painted metal, and your feet are ahead of the front wheel wells. The front axle is practically beneath your butt.

Unlike the workaday pickups you can rent from Home Depot and Menards, this truck, with its massive screen and power windows, is an ergonomic miracle compared with single-cab full-size rentals. Remember when steering wheels were only responsible for turning left and right and occasionally honking the horn? The Kei-01’s wheel is like that. Except the horn’s high-pitched beep is too humiliating to use in anger.

Your fingertips on the steering wheel are so close to the front of the vehicle that they could almost be the hood ornament. Which is certainly novel and makes it super easy to nose in close to objects. Though the lack of a crumple zone aft of your knuckles is a concern that flashes through your mind.

Around the little dirt loop, the Kei-01 offers a driving feel that’s akin to a riding lawn mower. The steering takes nearly 4.5 turns lock-to-lock, but the Kei-01 is still stupid-easy to maneuver. There’s a rawness about scooting around in it that makes you feel like you’re getting paid hourly. This workhorse may be at a speed disadvantage compared to most of the electric scooters in our Gear Team’s roundup, but try hauling hay with one of those.

See all results for used cars for sale near 19106

Underneath all that adorable sheetmetal is a 660-cc three-cylinder engine that sounds about as smooth as a Honda Grom. It’s paired with a continuously variable automatic transmission. Despite its goofy proportions, the Kei-01 isn’t as front-heavy as it looks. With the engine mounted near the middle of the truck, this little box on wheels feels balanced. It lacks a dedicated transfer case, but its four-wheel-drive system has an electronic lock mode to add a bit more confidence on hill climbs.

The best part might be the roughly five-and-a-half-foot bed. Its low load floor makes for a perfect bench, and all three bedsides fold down. Lower the tailgate, or either side, or all three. It’s brilliantly simple and quick. There’s no tall bedside to reach over, and you don’t have to climb into the bed to reach stuff. The truck can handle 600 pounds of cargo too. Seriously, why can’t full-size pickup beds offer this kind of flexibility?

We spent only a short time driving the little Kei-01, but even limited to 25 mph, it’s still rather compelling. And, unlike the used kei trucks imported from Japan, the Scion has a factory warranty. The big unknown still hanging over this small truck is the price, which Toyota hasn’t announced yet. When all you need is a little truck, without most of the drawbacks of a big one, the Kei-01 certainly fits.

#4251. 2026 Toyota GRMN Corolla First Drive: A Blur of Nür

Toyota’s most expensive Corolla ever bristles with track-focused hardware.

Slapping Turn 1’s bright-green curbing, it’s immediately clear that the GR team has done something really good. I’m driving the Toyota GRMN Corolla at Eagles Canyon Raceway in Texas, and the first 30 seconds of recorded voice notes are just me eagerly repeating “Aw, yeah” at various parts of the track.

The GRMN, which stands for “Gazoo Racing tuned by Meister of Nürburgring,” receives an incredible amount of attention for a car Toyota won’t build more than 730 of. The changes are as juicy as workplace gossip. Ten slots are cut into the underside of the carbon-fiber hood to direct air where Toyota says it will contribute to more predictable steering at high speeds. Engineers shortened the front suspension’s bump-stop stroke by four millimeters while adding two millimeters at the rear, helping the car settle over curbing. There’s also a taller first gear and a pinch more torque in the midrange. And finally, an optional oil cooler keeps the all-wheel-drive system happy.

See all results for new 2027 Toyota GR Corolla for sale near 30337

Toyota’s obsession over details is admirable. The GRMN’s improvements over the standard GR are so subtle that they may go unnoticed by most folks and even some car nerds. I started my track time with an automatic GR Corolla, then switched to the GRMN and back. While the car looks only slightly different, the driving experience is wildly new.

The steering is the first major giveaway. Immediately, the GRMN feels much tighter and more direct in turns than the regular GR Corolla. Turn-in is dramatically quicker, and return to center is noticeably stronger. Initially, I thought Toyota had maybe beefed up its steering-rack slider. Nope. It’s largely the same hardware, but with an aggressive electric power-steering calibration. Adding to the different steering feel is a thinner steering-wheel rim, because even if it saved GR engineers less than an ounce, it still counts.

But it’s the suspension that really shines here. Eagles Canyon is rife with elevation changes, including several corners with curbing that would upset the automatic GR and send it bouncing upon landing. But like a honey badger, the GRMN don’t care. There’s no ugly secondary motion; you certainly feel the curb, but the nose stays flat on impact. Toyota developed special monotube dampers with internal rebound springs to help maintain tire contact, while its bump-stop changes convince you corner exit speeds are higher than ever. It’s the most Porsche-like behavior I’ve experienced in any car that competes with a Hyundai Elantra.

It’s worth noting that the regular GR that I drove wore Michelin Pilot Sport 4S tires, while the GRMN was on much stickier Pilot Sport Cup 2s. Some of the additional grip and steering response is absolutely down to the rubber, but the way the suspension manages impacts and keeps the body under control is an improvement that can’t be credited to tires alone.

See all results for new 2027 Toyota GR Corolla for sale near 30337

There is one exception to the GRMN’s good times that not even GRMN chief engineer Naoyuki Sakamoto could explain. During quick countersteering inputs, the electric steering occasionally delivers an unnatural kick through the wheel. It feels as though the power assist has reached its limit, though just for a moment. We experienced it three times over at least 20 laps, but never during our street drive.

The GRMN uses that same ole G16E-GTS 300-hp turbocharged 1.6-liter three-cylinder. Torque increases by just seven pound-feet to 302, with Toyota concentrating the additional grunt between 4000 and 4600 rpm, where the engine spent much of its time at Eagles Canyon clawing out of corners.

The six-speed manual gets its own collection of changes. The close-ratio EA68F gearbox has a taller first gear and a shorter third gear, changing how the engine works through its powerband. Engineers even revised the shifter-cable mount to make the action more direct. Having driven a manual GR recently, the difference is obvious. It’s not Honda Civic Type R good, but it’s still really good.

The GRMN also has additional cooling hardware and a driver-actuated intercooler water-spray system. The only other car I’ve ever driven with one of these was the Subaru WRX STI S209, which would make for a rather interesting comparison test if Subaru still built it. A one-gallon water tank sits beneath the GRMN’s cargo floor, supplying enough water to spray the intercooler for approximately 150 seconds. Toyota claims this can lower intake temperatures by roughly 14 to 20 degrees Fahrenheit. Unfortunately, it’s somewhat difficult to see the status of the system, as there’s no indication in the gauge cluster. Instead, the small button has an even tinier amber light that blinks slowly while two nozzles spray water onto the intercooler. It’s no place to have your eyes pointed while setting lap times, and it left us prayin’ it was still sprayin’.

The most important update may be the optional oil cooler for the all-wheel-drive transfer unit. During Lightning Lap testing in regular GR Corollas at Virginia International Raceway, we’ve experienced overheating that triggers the dreaded “AWD System Overheated” warning. Toyota’s solution circulates gear oil through a separate heat exchanger using an electric pump, roughly doubling the system’s oil capacity in the process.

However, the cooler isn’t standard equipment, and installing it involves more than bolting on a few hoses. It requires an ECU reflash and activation procedure, as the system’s electrical demands also introduce a fuel-economy penalty. Toyota installed the accessory on our GRMN before we took it onto the circuit. Its own testing suggests the system will prevent the AWD system from ever entering 2WD mode. That’s promising, although even 20 laps at Eagles Canyon (with the front straight closed) aren’t enough to declare the problem solved. We’d love to see how it handles VIR’s 4.1-mile Grand Course.

Eventually, Toyota representatives politely suggested I take a break from lapping the GRMN, motioning toward the line of other journalists in the pits. Ugh, fine. Later, I got another turn behind the wheel for the drive from the track to the hotel. And what a completely different experience that was.

As in the GR Corolla Morizo Edition, Toyota has stripped the rear seats from this four-door hatchback as part of an effort to reduce weight by 66 pounds. The rear windows are fixed. There’s no rear wiper either, which Toyota says saves about two pounds.

The GRMN is incredibly loud on public roads. With the rear seats removed, there’s little separating the cabin from the racket coming from behind. Those Cup 2 tires scream over mixed asphalt, their noise changing pitch with every new section of pavement. On the highway, you find yourself yelling at the passenger next to you, and not because they started talking politics.

The ride is similarly uncompromising. The same suspension that so calmly devours curbing at Eagles Canyon can make ordinary pavement feel jarring. Even the steering, which I couldn’t stop praising on the circuit, takes some getting used to, as it’s so quick on the street, where small inputs produce immediate responses.

I guess that’s why they didn’t name it the Corolla GR Route 380.

The GRMN Corolla starts at $65,655, which is about $24K more than the standard car. That almost GR86-sized price gap is no small upcharge for a Corolla that’s heavy on track ability and light on everyday ability. It’s also interesting that of the 730 GRMN Corollas being built, none will be sold in Germany, home of the actual Nürburgring; it’s a Japan, Australia, and North America offering only.

At one point during the drive event, one of the GRMNs picked up a nail in its tire, and Toyota had to pull it from the drive rotation to give it fresh Michelins. Rather than sit around and pout (as journalists sometimes do), influencers and editors climbed into the regular automatic GR Corolla for a few laps. The lack of complaining during that inconvenience proves my next point.

The GRMN’s biggest rival is the regular GR Corolla. The new car’s tiny yet important improvements make it considerably better on track, but is a few tenths per lap worth $24K? Not to mention the street-driving inconveniences? Maybe, for some. For everyone else, there’s a perfectly good GR Corolla with rear seats that doesn’t require earplugs.

#4247. Without this protein, damaged muscle fills with fat and scar tissue

When muscles are injured, the body normally activates specialized stem cells that help rebuild damaged tissue. But scientists have discovered that without one critical protein, this repair system can break down, leaving injured muscles filled with fat and scar tissue instead of healthy muscle.

Researchers at the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania have identified an unexpected role for a protein called TRF2, which was previously known primarily for protecting chromosomes. Their findings suggest that TRF2 is also essential for maintaining the identity of muscle stem cells, allowing them to continue repairing and regenerating muscle throughout life.

The discovery, published in Science Advances, could provide new directions for muscular dystrophy treatments. It may also help scientists understand important differences between muscle regeneration and cancer, including why skeletal muscle can repair itself so effectively while cancers originating in muscle are relatively uncommon.

"For years, TRF2 has been viewed as a protein whose primary job is protecting the ends of chromosomes from damage or corruption," said senior author Foteini Mourkioti, PhD, an associate professor of Orthopedic Surgery at Penn Medicine. "But rather than simply protecting DNA, TRF2 seems to be key to regenerating muscle throughout life."

A Hidden Protein With an Unexpected Role in Muscle Repair

For years, scientists have studied TRF2 because of its role in safeguarding telomeres, the protective structures found at the ends of chromosomes. Chromosomes carry our genetic information, and telomeres help keep their ends from deteriorating or being mistaken for damaged DNA.

The new research shows that TRF2 has another important responsibility. It helps muscle stem cells retain the genetic instructions that make them muscle stem cells in the first place. Maintaining that identity is essential because these specialized cells serve as the body's reserve supply for repairing injured muscle.

Under normal conditions, muscle stem cells spend much of their time inactive. When an injury occurs, they become active, multiply, and help replace damaged muscle tissue. Some then return to a resting state, preserving a population of stem cells that can respond to future injuries.

Through laboratory experiments, the researchers found that TRF2 levels change as muscle stem cells move between these different stages. The protein's activity rises and falls as the cells transition from dormancy to repair and then replenish themselves, suggesting that TRF2 helps regulate the entire regeneration process.

Without TRF2, Damaged Muscles Accumulate Fat and Scar Tissue

To understand how important TRF2 is, the scientists removed the protein from muscle stem cells in laboratory mice. At first, the animals' muscles appeared normal, suggesting that the loss of TRF2 did not immediately damage existing muscle tissue.

Over time, however, a serious problem emerged. The population of functional muscle stem cells began to decline, leaving the animals increasingly unable to repair damaged muscle.

The researchers initially expected the cells to die, since losing TRF2 can produce that outcome in other tissues. Instead, they discovered something more surprising: the cells remained alive but lost the molecular identity that allowed them to function as muscle stem cells.

In effect, the cells no longer maintained the biological program needed to perform their specialized repair duties.

The consequences became clear when the muscles were injured. Rather than rebuilding healthy muscle, the damaged tissue accumulated fat and scar tissue, a form of tissue replacement that cannot restore normal muscle function.

"This completely changes how we think about TRF2's role in these cells," said Mourkioti. "The loss of identity has severe implications for whether recovery from injury is even possible."

A Potential Breakthrough for Muscular Dystrophy Research

The team also investigated whether TRF2 plays a role in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a serious inherited disorder that causes progressive muscle weakness and degeneration. The disease interferes with the body's ability to maintain healthy muscles, making effective repair especially important.

Using a mouse model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the researchers removed TRF2 from muscle stem cells and observed a dramatic worsening of the disease.

Muscle degeneration progressed much faster, and the affected mice had shorter survival times. These findings indicate that TRF2 plays an important role in preserving the regenerative capacity of muscles already struggling with a serious genetic disease.

The results do not yet establish a new treatment for muscular dystrophy. However, they identify a biological mechanism that researchers may eventually be able to target to help preserve muscle stem cell function and improve tissue repair.

How TRF2 Protects the Identity of Muscle Stem Cells

Further experiments revealed how TRF2 performs this unexpected function.

Although the protein is best known for working at the ends of chromosomes, the researchers found that it also attaches to regulatory regions throughout the genome. These regions help control which genes are active or inactive, determining how cells behave and what specialized functions they perform.

For muscle stem cells, this regulation is particularly important. Their ability to repair muscle depends on maintaining a specific pattern of gene activity that preserves their identity and regenerative potential.

The scientists discovered that many of the DNA regions associated with TRF2 contain unusual structures known as G-quadruplexes. These structures form when sections of DNA rich in the building block guanine fold into distinctive arrangements involving four interacting strands or segments.

G-quadruplexes have attracted considerable scientific interest because they can influence how genes function. They are also being investigated as possible targets for cancer treatments.

The Penn researchers found that TRF2 interacts with these specialized DNA structures to help maintain the genetic program that keeps muscle stem cells functioning properly.

"We found that TRF2 works through these secondary DNA structures to preserve the identity of muscle stem cells and keep them capable of repairing damaged muscle," Mourkioti said. "That was completely unexpected."

What Muscle Regeneration Could Reveal About Cancer

Beyond muscular dystrophy, the discovery may help researchers investigate a longstanding mystery about muscle biology.

Skeletal muscle, the type of muscle that allows the body to move, has an impressive ability to regenerate after injury. Yet cancers that originate in skeletal muscle are relatively rare, even though other tissues with substantial regenerative activity can be more vulnerable to cancer.

This raises an important question: how can muscle maintain such a powerful repair system without frequently developing cancer?

The researchers believe that TRF2's unusual role in muscle stem cells could offer clues. By examining how the protein regulates gene activity in muscle compared with other tissues, scientists may gain a better understanding of the mechanisms that support regeneration while limiting the risk of uncontrolled cell growth.

That distinction matters because cancer develops when cells acquire changes that allow them to grow and divide without the normal biological restraints. Finding ways to strengthen muscle repair without encouraging abnormal growth would be an important goal for future therapies.

Mourkioti and her colleagues are now investigating whether the way muscle stem cells use TRF2 could lead to new treatment strategies for muscular dystrophy. They also hope to determine what this mechanism can reveal about cancer biology in tissues that are more susceptible to the disease.

Although additional research is needed to determine whether these findings can be translated into treatments for people, the discovery reveals an important part of the body's muscle repair system. It also demonstrates that a protein long associated with protecting DNA has a much broader role in keeping muscles capable of healing.

The research was supported by grants from the National Institutes of Health/ National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases (R01 DK123356, R01s CA174904, GM101149, and FDN-143330).

#4244. Escape From Tarkov Reveals Top Down Spin-Off

Escape From Tarkov is celebrating its first anniversary since leaving what once felt like eternal early access last November. Now that the hard part of the journey is over, Battlestate Games and director Nikita Buyanov are looking at the future, and that means new games.

As reported by Grant Taylor-Hill of Insider Gaming, the next chapter for the Escape From Tarkov developer is still going to be an extraction shooter, but it will be a lot different from the game that started it all.

Nikita Buyanov told Insider Gaming that part of the future for the Escape From Tarkov creator lies on mobile.

According to Buyanov, this game will “look and feel like Tarkov.” Details are scarce for the time being, but it has now been confirmed that the next game will be a mobile-based, top-down extraction shooter set in the world of Escape From Tarkov.

Ubisoft reportedly has a new Rainbow Six: Vegas game in the works, with a third entry considered more likely than a remake.

Although it may sound strange to someone who’s only familiar with ‘classic’ Tarkov, the concept has been thoroughly validated through Team Soda’s Escape From Duckov. The game, endorsed by Battlestate Games, is an avian-themed parody of Escape From Tarkov, with an engaging gameplay loop and endearing art style.

According to Buyanov, this game will “look and feel like Tarkov.”

Games like Hotline Miami, the original Helldivers, and the Intravenous series have shown you can deliver plenty of grittiness and tense action with a top-down perspective. The medium’s possibilities are endless, so it is up to Battlestate Games to work out how to capture the magic of Escape From Tarkov and bring it to mobile.

A release date for the Escape From Tarkov mobile spin-off has not been announced yet, but you can probably expect it before the elusive hideout management app for the core game.

Battlestate Games is also currently working on a single-player title, which some players have assumed to be a substitute for the Russia 2028 project that’s currently on hold.

Shortly after delivering Escape From Tarkov to the world in its final form, Nikita Buyanov announced his next project, Fragmentary Order.

According to the Russian auteur, Fragmentary Order is “almost there,” and marketing materials shared by the game’s official page certainly seem to reflect that.

The game takes Escape From Tarkov’s hardcore shooter mechanics into the one place that hasn’t been corrupted by capitalism, and expands the kind of corporate-infused chaos from Tarkov into the entire solar system.

Pre-orders are already open for Fragmentary Order, divided between Candidates ($44.99) and Founders tiers ($79.99). Both versions grant access to closed alpha testing.

Besides Buyanov, other Escape From Tarkov alumni are also making a name for themselves in new projects. Tarkov veterans Dmitry Ogorodnikov, Jean Tyulegenov, and German Terekhov have moved on to found Nomion Games and are currently working on a cyberpunk shooter titled Rush is Real.

The art direction has been handed over to Croatian 3D artist Space Meerkat, who is famous for his elaborate cyberpunk concepts.

Rush is Real does not have a release window yet, but you can follow development updates here.

With no particular preamble, Asha Sharma revealed that MachineGames has begun work on the next mainline Wolfenstein title.

The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1.
